questions.prompt: Create a function `delay(ms)` that returns a new Promise which resolves after `ms` milliseconds. Then write an async function `greetAfterDelay(name)` that awaits `delay(1000)` and then logs 'Hello, [name]!'. Call it with 'Amara'.

Create a function `fetchUser(id)` that returns a new Promise. If id > 0, resolve after 500ms with `{id, name: 'User ' + id}`. If id <= 0, reject with Error('Invalid ID'). Write an async function that calls fetchUser(1) and fetchUser(-1) using try/catch, logging success or the error message for each.
What is the difference between writing `await promise` inside a try/catch vs using `.then().catch()`? When would you prefer one over the other?
questions.sample_answer: Both handle the same resolved/rejected states. `await` with try/catch makes async code look synchronous — it flows top-to-bottom, errors are caught in the same way as sync errors, and you can put multiple awaits in one try block. `.then().catch()` chains callbacks — each step returns a new promise, and the chain can become hard to follow with many steps. Prefer async/await when: (1) you have sequential steps that depend on each other, (2) you want readable, flat code, (3) you need complex control flow (loops, conditionals). Prefer .then() when: (1) you're doing a single fetch-and-process without complex logic, (2) you want to attach a handler without creating an async function, (3) you're working with older code that already uses .then() chains.

questions.prompt: Write an async function that uses Promise.all to fetch 3 values in parallel: `delay(300).then(() => 'A')`, `delay(200).then(() => 'B')`, `delay(100).then(() => 'C')`. Log the results array. Note: they should all arrive together despite different delays.

Write an async function that processes an array of 3 names sequentially: for each name, await a 200ms delay, then log 'Processed: [name]'. After all are done, log 'All done!'. Use a for...of loop with await inside.
What is Promise.all and when would you use it instead of awaiting each promise sequentially? What happens if one of the promises in Promise.all rejects?
questions.sample_answer: Promise.all takes an array of promises and returns a single promise that resolves with an array of all results when ALL promises resolve. Use it when you have multiple independent async operations that don't depend on each other — fetching user data AND post data simultaneously instead of one after the other. It's faster because all operations run concurrently. If ONE promise rejects, the entire Promise.all rejects immediately with that error — the other results are discarded (though the operations still complete in the background). For handling mixed success/failure, use Promise.allSettled instead — it waits for all promises and returns an array of {status, value/reason} objects.

questions.prompt: What are the three states of a Promise? Can a Promise change from resolved to rejected or vice versa? Explain.
questions.sample_answer: The three states are: (1) Pending — the initial state; the async operation hasn't completed yet. (2) Fulfilled (resolved) — the operation completed successfully; the promise has a result value. (3) Rejected — the operation failed; the promise has a reason (error). A promise can only transition ONCE: from pending to fulfilled, or from pending to rejected. Once it settles (fulfilled or rejected), it NEVER changes state again. Calling resolve() after reject() (or vice versa) has no effect — the first one wins. This immutability is a key design principle: consumers of the promise can rely on the result being stable. Once you have a value from .then() or await, it won't suddenly become an error later.

questions.prompt: Create a function `timeout(ms)` that returns a Promise which rejects after ms milliseconds with Error('Timeout!'). Use Promise.race to race a slow operation (resolves in 2000ms with 'Done!') against a timeout(1000). Log whichever wins. Then race again with timeout(3000) — this time the operation should win.

Write an async function that fetches data from 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1' using fetch with async/await (not .then()). Check response.ok, parse the JSON, and log the user's name. Wrap in try/catch and log any errors.
Why can't you use `await` at the top level of a regular script (outside an async function)? What is the workaround?
questions.sample_answer: `await` is only valid inside an async function because it pauses execution of that function while the promise resolves. At the top level of a regular script, there's no function to pause — the script is expected to run synchronously to completion. If await could pause the top level, it would block the entire main thread. Workarounds: (1) Wrap your code in an async IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression): `(async () => { const data = await fetchData(); })();` (2) Create a named async function and call it: `async function main() { ... } main();` (3) In modern environments with ES modules (type='module' in HTML or .mjs files), top-level await IS supported because modules are loaded asynchronously by design.

questions.prompt: Write a function `withRetry(asyncFn, maxRetries)` that calls asyncFn. If it rejects, retry up to maxRetries times. Log each attempt. If all retries fail, throw the last error. Test it with a function that fails twice then succeeds on attempt 3.

Use Promise.all to fetch two URLs in parallel: 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1' and 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?userId=1&_limit=3'. Parse both, then log the user's name and the number of posts. Use async/await throughout.
What is the difference between `Promise.all`, `Promise.allSettled`, and `Promise.race`? Give a use case for each.
questions.sample_answer: `Promise.all(promises)` — resolves when ALL promises resolve (returns array of results). Rejects immediately if ANY promise rejects. Use case: loading a dashboard that needs user data AND settings AND notifications — all must succeed for the page to render. `Promise.allSettled(promises)` — waits for ALL promises to settle (resolve or reject). Returns array of {status: 'fulfilled', value} or {status: 'rejected', reason} objects. Use case: sending emails to 100 recipients — you want to know which succeeded and which failed, without one failure cancelling the rest. `Promise.race(promises)` — resolves/rejects with whichever promise settles FIRST. Use case: implementing a timeout — race your actual fetch against a timer; if the timer fires first, you know the fetch took too long.
